title: Crime at a Crossroads: Eastern and South-Eastern Asia
summary: Maya and Daniel unpack the 2025 Global Organized Crime Index report from GI-TOC focusing on Eastern and South-Eastern Asia. They examine the stark regional contrasts, the explosion of industrial cyber-scam compounds and human trafficking, and the world's widest resilience gaps.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Hello and welcome. Today we are digging into a major new regional report from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, or GI-TOC. It is part of their 2025 Global Organized Crime Index, and this specific release is titled Eastern Asia and South-Eastern Asia: Crime at a crossroads.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And if you are working in regional security, illicit finance, supply chain compliance, or counter-trafficking policy, this is one of those benchmark assessments you really cannot ignore. The sheer scale covered here is staggering.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It really is. The report looks across sixteen countries that house about 2.32 billion people. That is nearly half of Asia's entire population and roughly twenty-eight percent of the global total. And Asia as a whole actually presents a very striking paradox in the 2025 Index: the continent records the highest average criminality score of any continent on earth, yet it ranks only fourth globally when it comes to resilience.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Right, but once you zoom into the sub-regions, Eastern Asia and South-Eastern Asia could hardly look more different, could they? They are geographical neighbours, but their trajectories are moving in almost opposite directions.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. South-Eastern Asia sits well above the global average across criminality, criminal markets, and criminal actors, while falling below the global average for resilience. In fact, out of the twenty-two regions evaluated globally in the Index, South-Eastern Asia ranks fifth highest for criminality, with an overall criminality score of 5.91.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And compare that to Eastern Asia, which ranks fourteenth out of twenty-two globally with a criminality score of 4.74. What caught my eye immediately in the data is that Eastern Asia is actually one of the few regions in the entire world where criminality has dropped since the first Index edition back in 2021.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: That is a huge point. In 2021, Eastern Asia's criminality stood at 4.85, then 4.80 in 2023, and now down to 4.74 in 2025. Meanwhile, South-Eastern Asia climbed from 5.45 in 2021 to 5.81 in 2023, and up to 5.91 in 2025. And its resilience dropped over that same timeframe, from 4.58 in 2021 down to 4.44 in 2025.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Before we unpack what is driving those numbers, let us touch quickly on the methodology, because GI-TOC notes a comparability caveat that listeners should understand when looking at changes between 2021 and 2025.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, absolutely. In the 2021 edition, the Index evaluated ten criminal markets and four criminal-actor types. For the 2023 and 2025 editions, they expanded the scope to fifteen markets and five actor types. That meant adding cyber-dependent crimes, financial crimes, counterfeit goods, illicit trade in excisable goods, and extortion and protection racketeering, alongside private-sector actors. So the report is careful to explain that part of the score increases between 2021 and 2023 reflects this wider lens, though cross-country comparisons remain fully valid because every country was assessed under the exact same expanded framework.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That context is critical, especially when we look at individual country shifts. Take Singapore, for instance. Singapore saw its criminality score rise by 0.59 between 2021 and 2025. But that does not mean street crime suddenly exploded in Singapore.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Not at all. The report specifically highlights that Singapore's increase stems from the inclusion of financial and cyber-dependent crimes. It mirrors a broader global pattern where major international financial centres are inherently exposed to illicit financial flows and digital fraud. Despite that bump, Singapore still boasts the second-highest resilience score in Asia and ranks tenth globally, with a resilience score of 7.79.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Now, let us get into the countries that saw the most dramatic increases. The report pulls no punches here: Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar have seen their illicit economies surge on an unprecedented scale.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: They really have. Between 2021 and 2025, Cambodia saw its criminality score increase by 1.19 points, Laos increased by 0.86, and Myanmar rose by 0.49. In fact, Cambodia recorded a 1.80-point jump in its criminal actors score alone, which the authors point out is the largest increase for any country in the entire world.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And Myanmar's overall position in the Index is just staggering. It literally sits at the absolute extremes of the entire global assessment.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It does. Out of all 193 UN member states evaluated, Myanmar has the highest criminality score in the world, and the lowest resilience score in the world, sitting at just 1.46. And look at the trend line: Myanmar's resilience dropped by 1.96 points between 2021 and 2025. Its criminal actor score is 8.50, and its criminal market score is 7.67.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: What is underpinning this massive surge across the Mekong region? The report points squarely at the explosion of industrial-scale cyber-scam operations.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. Cyber-scam compounds operating in Cambodia, Myanmar, and Laos have created what the report describes as a triple threat of converging criminal markets: cyber-dependent crimes, financial crimes, and human trafficking. In these compounds, people are trafficked and coerced under horrific conditions into running online fraud, while the profits feed sophisticated laundering operations.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the human trafficking data in the report really reflects that shift. Look at Figure 9 in the study. In Myanmar, the human trafficking score jumped from 6.50 in 2021 to 9.00 in 2025. That is a 2.50-point increase. In Cambodia, it rose from 7.50 to 8.50. And in Laos, it climbed from 6.50 to 8.00.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And think about what that means structurally: historically, countries like Laos and Myanmar were primarily sources and transit points for human trafficking. Now, because of these scam compounds and special economic zones, they have become major destination markets as well. Men, women, and children are forced into cyber-scam operations, forced labour, and sex work. And the report notes that special economic zones in particular have become convergence hubs where multiple criminal markets intersect.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let us talk about the specific criminal markets in South-Eastern Asia more broadly, because the report breaks down five distinct markets that are driving the region's elevated criminality.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, Figure 8 lays this out very clearly. First is the synthetic drug trade. South-Eastern Asia scores 7.41, which is 2.27 points above the global average of 5.14. That ranks South-Eastern Asia third out of all twenty-two regions in the world. The report notes this is driven by the massive methamphetamine economy, alongside growing diversification into substances like ketamine and etomidate.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And then environmental crimes. South-Eastern Asia actually ranks number one globally in two environmental categories, doesn't it?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It ranks first in the world for fauna crimes, with a score of 7.23 compared to the global average of 4.90, largely propelled by wildlife trafficking. And it ranks first in the world for flora crimes at 6.09 versus the global average of 4.02, driven primarily by illegal logging. Then you have cyber-dependent crimes, where the region scores 6.41 and ranks fourth globally. And finally, the heroin trade, where it scores 5.41, ranking third globally. In addition, financial crimes are the region's second-highest scoring market overall, and counterfeit goods score relatively high across many countries.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: There is also a very interesting exception mentioned for both Eastern and South-Eastern Asia when it comes to illicit drug flows. Cocaine, right?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. Both regions score well below the global average for the cocaine trade. So while cocaine markets have surged in many other parts of the world, Eastern and South-Eastern Asia have largely diverged from that global trend.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Now, turning to Eastern Asia's markets, the report points out that while Eastern Asia scores below global averages for most illicit markets, there are two countries heavily driving regional scores: China and the DPRK.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: That is right. China and North Korea are the primary drivers for cyber-dependent crimes and the synthetic drug trade in Eastern Asia. The report notes that China also records high scores for flora crimes, specifically illegal timber trafficking, and fauna crimes, including trafficking wildlife products for traditional medicine, food, fashion, and the exotic pet trade. Plus, China remains a major global hub for counterfeit goods. North Korea, on the other hand, records particularly high scores for arms trafficking and human trafficking.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let us pivot to the criminal actors involved, because this is where the governance breakdown becomes painfully clear. In South-Eastern Asia, who is actually running these markets?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The report highlights several key actor categories. First and foremost are state-embedded actors. Myanmar and Cambodia both score a staggering 9.0 out of 10 for state-embedded actors. Indonesia and the Philippines are not far behind, both scoring 8.0 out of 10. Mafia-style groups also score highly, especially in Myanmar and the Philippines. And then there are foreign criminal actors.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And South-Eastern Asia is the second-highest scoring region in the entire world for foreign criminal actors, trailing only West Africa. Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar are heavily penetrated by foreign criminal networks. South-Eastern Asia also scores well above the global average for private-sector actors involved in organized crime.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: In Eastern Asia, by contrast, the picture is almost inverted. Eastern Asia scores below the global average across all five criminal actor types, ranking eighteenth globally for foreign actors. But there is one glaring, extreme exception: the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Where the state-embedded actor score hits a perfect ten out of ten.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: A full 10 out of 10. The DPRK's overall criminality score is moderate, at 5.47 for markets and 3.90 for actors, because its conventional domestic illicit markets are relatively closed off. But when it comes to state-embedded criminality and cyber operations, it is exceptionally high.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let us look at resilience, because this is where the report draws some of its most compelling conclusions. Both of these regions display what the authors describe as extreme polarization.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Polarization that actually exceeds any other region in the world. Look at Eastern Asia: you have the Republic of Korea, which has a resilience score of 8.00, the highest in the entire region and one of the top scores globally. Japan is right behind it at 7.50. But on the same peninsula, you have North Korea with a resilience score of 1.63, the third-lowest in the world. That is a massive 6.37-point resilience gap between two neighbouring countries.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And you see almost the exact same chasm in South-Eastern Asia between Singapore at 7.79 and Myanmar at 1.46. That is a 6.33-point spread.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It demonstrates just how uneven state capacity is across these territories. When you look at South-Eastern Asia's institutional weaknesses, the report pinpoints three areas where the region falls furthest below global norms: relations with non-state actors, which averages just 3.50; government transparency and accountability, at 3.86; and judicial systems and detention, at 4.00.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Those are serious institutional deficits. Were there any resilience indicators in South-Eastern Asia that actually managed to beat the global average?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Only two: anti-money laundering and economic regulatory capacity, both of which scored just slightly above the global average. The region's highest scoring resilience indicators overall were international cooperation and national policies and laws, but even those still sat below their respective global averages.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And what about the middle of the pack? In Figure 7, the vulnerability quadrant plot, the report points out some interesting middle-tier dynamics.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, Thailand and Vietnam are highlighted as countries to watch because their resilience scores are very close to the global average. Vietnam is at 4.79 and Thailand is at 4.96, right on the threshold. The authors specifically suggest that targeted, strategic improvements in resilience could elevate both Thailand and Vietnam into the high-resilience quadrant.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And then you have Malaysia and China, which occupy that quadrant with above-average criminality, but also above-average resilience. China scores 6.63 for markets, 6.00 for actors, and 5.54 for resilience. Malaysia is 6.57 for markets, 6.50 for actors, and 5.71 for resilience.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. And on China's resilience profile, the report notes an interesting nuance: China sits around the global mean for government transparency and accountability, and victim and witness support, but it falls well below the global average when it comes to relations with non-state actors, meaning independent civil society.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And then on the flip side, you have Brunei and Timor-Leste, which have relatively low criminality, but below-average resilience frameworks.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Brunei scores 3.20 on markets and 2.60 on actors, with 4.63 resilience. Timor-Leste is at 3.47 for markets, 4.50 for actors, and 3.88 for resilience. And we should also mention the positive movers. Two countries managed to simultaneously reduce criminality and improve resilience between 2021 and 2025: the Republic of Korea and the Philippines.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That is worth emphasizing. The Philippines reduced its criminality score by 0.27 while improving its resilience score by 0.33. And South Korea reduced criminality by 0.49 while boosting its resilience by 0.46. That shows progress is entirely possible, even in complex regional operating environments.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It really does. But the overarching takeaway from the report is that the region as a whole sits at a critical crossroads. The rapid industrialization of cyber-scam operations in Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar is not just a localized problem; it has transnational tentacles reaching into global financial systems and ensnaring victims from all over the world.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And because state-embedded actors in those hub countries are so deeply entrenched, scoring 9.0 out of 10, traditional law enforcement cooperation faces structural roadblocks from the inside.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Which is why the authors stress the critical importance of understanding both national nuances and cross-border regional dynamics. You cannot treat Eastern Asia and South-Eastern Asia as a monolith, nor can you tackle cyber-fraud or human trafficking without addressing the governance vacuums and corruption that allow these hubs to flourish.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So looking ahead, what should our listeners be watching for next?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Keep a close eye on whether countries like Thailand and Vietnam can implement those targeted institutional reforms to lift their resilience into the upper tier. Watch how the international community responds to the cyber-scam compounds and special economic zones in the Mekong. And GI-TOC notes that a forthcoming companion report will examine trends across Western Asia, Southern Asia, and Central Asia and the Caucasus, which will complete the broader Asian picture.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: A vital piece of analysis on a rapidly shifting landscape. Thank you, Maya.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Thank you, Daniel. And thank you all for listening. We will catch you in the next deep dive.
